summary: Specifies the DetNet IP data plane when running over an IEEE 802.1 Time-Sensitive Networking sub-network. It defines no new procedures, taking its statements from normative text in other RFCs.

plainLanguage.summary: Shows how time-guaranteed IP traffic rides on special local networks designed for exact timing.

questions: how does detnet use time sensitive networking
how does detnet ip work over tsn
how do you map ip flows to tsn streams
subtitle: Running guaranteed IP traffic over specialized local networks

tldr.problem: Networks need to carry IP traffic with strict timing guarantees, requiring both IP-layer reliability and Layer 2 coordination.
tldr.mechanism: DetNet IP maps individual IP flows to IEEE 802.1 TSN streams, allowing TSN's timing and protection mechanisms to serve DetNet requirements.
tldr.outcome: Organizations can run time-critical IP applications across bridged networks designed for deterministic delivery.

facts.label: Flow identification
facts.value: 6-tuple (source IP, dest IP, protocol, source port, dest port)

today: RFC 9023 is informational, defining how DetNet IP works when routed through IEEE 802.1 TSN sub-networks. The mappings and requirements in this RFC allow the two standards to interoperate.

sections.title: What DetNet and TSN Are
sections.content:
DetNet provides networks with extremely low packet loss and bounded delivery latency for critical applications. This RFC focuses on the scenario where DetNet nodes (hosts and routers) are connected across an IEEE 802.1 TSN sub-network.

TSN is a set of IEEE standards that add timing guarantees and redundancy to Layer 2 (bridged) networks. DetNet and TSN both aim to reduce jitter and loss, but they operate at different layers: DetNet at Layer 3 (IP), TSN at Layer 2 (Ethernet).
sections.plainLanguage: Think of DetNet as a guarantee: your data will arrive in time. TSN is the tool that actually provides that on a local network. This RFC explains how they work together.

sections.title: The Mapping Between Layers
sections.content:
DetNet decomoses into two sub-layers: the service sub-layer (packet protection via replication and elimination) and the forwarding sub-layer (congestion protection). Inside a TSN sub-network, DetNet IP routers receive and send flows that must be converted to and from TSN terms.

A DetNet flow is identified by a 6-tuple: source IP, destination IP, protocol, source port, destination port, and possibly other fields. TSN uses its own stream identification based on Ethernet headers and VLAN tags. At the edge of the TSN sub-network, DetNet nodes use conversion functions to map between these two identification schemes.
sections.plainLanguage: DetNet is like addressing a package. TSN is like shipping it. At each end of the shipping path, you need to convert from one system to the other.

sections.title: How TSN-Aware Nodes Behave
sections.content:
A TSN-aware DetNet node acts like two components: an IP DetNet node that the outside world sees, and a TSN talker or listener inside the sub-network. The node must support stream identification (recognizing which IP flows need which TSN treatment) and sequence encoding if frame replication and elimination for redundancy (FRER) is enabled in the TSN sub-network.

DetNet IP nodes that are not TSN-aware can still work; the TSN relay nodes modify Ethernet headers to handle the conversion. However, TSN-aware nodes provide tighter control and can better coordinate between the two domains.
sections.plainLanguage: A node can speak both languages: it knows how to be an IP router and how to be a TSN device. This bilingual ability helps data move smoothly from one domain to the other.

sections.title: Configuration and Control
sections.content:
Operators must provision DetNet IP configuration (per RFC 8939), TSN configuration (per IEEE standards), and the mapping between DetNet flows and TSN streams. This mapping tells the network which IP 6-tuple should use which TSN stream ID.

A key challenge is that DetNet and TSN use different control plane protocols: DetNet typically uses RSVP-TE, while TSN uses the Multiple Stream Registration Protocol (MSRP). Converting flow parameters from one domain to the other requires careful engineering, since a one-hop TSN sub-network may have very different delay and bandwidth characteristics than the full end-to-end DetNet path.
sections.plainLanguage: Someone has to tell both networks about the deal: which DetNet flows get mapped to which TSN streams, and what performance they promise.

sections.title: Security of the Connection
sections.content: The TSN sub-network should be subject to confidentiality and authentication protections. Knowing which DetNet/TSN services a sub-network provides can reveal operational details useful for attacks. Layer 2 security mechanisms defined by IEEE, such as MACsec (Media Access Control Security), can protect the connection between DetNet nodes and the TSN sub-network.
sections.plainLanguage: Since the link between DetNet nodes and the TSN network is important, it needs to be locked down. MACsec is IEEE's way of encrypting Layer 2 traffic.
